title: A New Approach to Monitoring Exercise Training
authors: Foster C, Florhaug JA, Franklin J, Gottschall L, Hrovatin LA, Parker S, Doleshal P, Dodge C
journal: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
population: Subjects (not further described in the abstract) who did steady-state and interval cycle exercise in part 1 and practised basketball in part 2; different subjects in each part
findings: Session RPE was compared with an objective heart-rate-based method for quantifying exercise during steady-state and interval cycling and during basketball practice.

During cycling the relationship between session-RPE score and HR score was highly consistent, although the absolute session-RPE score was significantly greater than the HR score; basketball showed the same pattern (consistent relationship, significantly greater absolute session-RPE score).
Despite different subjects in the two parts, the regression relationships between the two methods were nearly overlapping, which the authors read as broad applicability.
The authors conclude session RPE is a valid method of quantifying exercise training across a wide variety of exercise types and may be a mode- and intensity-independent method.
limitations: Criterion is an HR-based score (itself a proxy), not a physiological or performance outcome. Cycling and basketball only; no runners and no ultra-endurance exercise. The abstract gives no sample size, correlation coefficients or the CR-10 rating timing. The abstract does not spell out the duration x rating calculation (standard definition, taken from the full-text method, which was not read). Absolute session-RPE values are systematically higher than the HR method, so the scales are not interchangeable.
implications: Implement session-RPE load = session duration (min) x CR-10 rating (0-10) as the primary device-independent internal-load metric, since it works with no HR data (treadmill without strap, hot, hilly, trail).
Collect one rating per run after the session. The commonly used protocol asks about 30 min post-session, but the abstract does not state timing, so treat 30 min as a design default (grade D).

Store HR-based load separately from sRPE and never add them, because absolute values differ between methods. Interpret sRPE against the user's own history; do not apply a fixed cross-method conversion.

verification.notes: Crossref confirms title, JSCR, Feb 2001, first author Foster. Europe PMC does not index the Crossref DOI directly (lists legacy DOI 10.1519/1533-4287(2001)015<0109:anatme>2.0.co;2), so the abstract was fetched by PMID 11708692 and read.
